title: Assisting the Grading of a Handwritten General Chemistry Exam with Artificial Intelligence
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether an AI-based grading system can reliably assist with scoring a handwritten, high-stakes general chemistry exam. The core question is how closely AI-assigned scores match human grading across different types of exam responses, including chemical reactions, short and long open-ended text, numerical derivations, symbolic expressions, drawings, and graphing tasks. The study is motivated by the challenge of scaling open-ended assessment in STEM while maintaining reliability, fairness, and trust.

The authors implemented a multimodal AI grading workflow using an OpenAI model accessed through Azure AI Services. Student exam pages and corresponding rubric pages were uploaded as images, and the AI graded each page in structured JSON output. The study compared AI-assigned points with TA-assigned points treated as the operational ground truth, using linear regression, multiclass exact-match metrics, inter-run reliability measures, and filtering strategies such as partial-credit thresholds, item-response-theory-based risk thresholds, and exclusion of graphical task types. A human-in-the-loop framing was central to the approach, with the goal of using AI for routine grading while deferring uncertain cases to human graders.

The study took place in a large-enrollment undergraduate general chemistry course for non-majors at ETH Zurich in Switzerland. The sample included 296 consenting students out of 459 enrolled students, and all exams were handwritten and administered in German. The grading context involved 46 exam parts across 15 pages, with traditional TA grading conducted in parallel and used for comparison. Sixteen teaching assistants graded the exams under instructor supervision, with rubric calibration and auditing procedures described.

The main conclusion is that AI grading shows strong promise for some assessment formats but is not reliable enough to replace human graders in high-stakes settings without selective oversight. Agreement with human grading was highest for textual responses and chemical reaction questions, while performance was weaker for numerical, drawing, and graphing tasks. Aggregate total exam scores correlated strongly with human totals, and repeated AI runs were highly consistent, but item-level errors remained substantial enough to require filtering and human review. The authors conclude that AI can meaningfully reduce grading workload for routine assessment tasks, especially when paired with confidence-based deferral, but fairness, student trust, and careful oversight remain essential.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family multimodal reasoning model used via Azure AI Services for image-and-text processing and rubric-based scoring.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to grade scanned handwritten pages of a high-stakes general chemistry exam by comparing each student exam page image with the corresponding rubric page and outputting JSON point assignments for each problem part; specifically the paper used an OpenAI model ('gpt-o4-mini/high-vision'), normalized here to ChatGPT.

findings.finding_summary: AI grading processed 13,616 problem parts from 296 consenting students (4,440 pages) in about three hours using up to 30 parallel agents, at approximately $100 total token cost. The paper contrasts this with traditional human grading for the full 459-student exam, estimated at about 80 TA-hours and ≈$3,500, indicating strong efficiency gains for routine assessment workflows.
findings.measure: grading time and estimated grading cost

findings.finding_summary: Run-to-run consistency for AI-generated total scores was high, with ICC(A,1)=0.967 for a single run and ICC(A,5)=0.993 when averaging five runs. The within-target repeatability SD was Sw=1.92 points and the 95% repeatability coefficient was RC=5.33 points; Kendall's W=0.959 and pairwise Lin's CCC on totals had median 0.977 (IQR 0.045), showing stable totals despite some residual variation.
findings.measure: inter-run reliability of AI-assigned total scores
findings.effect_size: ICC(A,1)=0.967; ICC(A,5)=0.993; Sw=1.92 points; RC=5.33 points; Kendall's W=0.959; Lin's CCC median 0.977

findings.finding_summary: At the finer item×student level, agreement across five AI runs was lower but still strong: ICC(A,1)=0.836 and ICC(A,5)=0.962, with Sw=0.25 points and RC=0.68 points per cell. This indicates that small cell-level jitter exists, but much of it cancels out when scores are aggregated into exam totals.
findings.measure: inter-run reliability of AI-assigned rubric-cell scores
findings.effect_size: ICC(A,1)=0.836; ICC(A,5)=0.962; Sw=0.25 points; RC=0.68 points

findings.finding_summary: Unfiltered agreement between AI and TA grading on total exam scores was high but not sufficient for autonomous high-stakes grading, with regression slope=0.76, intercept=2.9, and R²=0.91. Per-problem R² ranged from 0.61 to 0.85, showing that total-score aggregation improved alignment relative to individual problems through partial cancellation of item-level errors.
findings.measure: agreement between AI-assigned and TA-assigned exam scores
findings.effect_size: Total-score slope=0.76, intercept=2.9, R²=0.91; per-problem R²=0.61-0.85

findings.finding_summary: Exact-match multiclass grading performance varied by response type. F1 was highest for long answer (0.68), short answer (0.60), and reaction questions (0.59), while graphing was weakest at F1=0.12 with normed F1=-0.098; overall across all 46 parts, Accuracy=0.64, Precision=0.31, Recall=0.29, F1=0.30, and normed F1=0.27.
findings.measure: multiclass exact-match grading quality by question type
findings.effect_size: Long answer F1=0.68; short answer F1=0.60; reaction F1=0.59; graphing F1=0.12; overall Accuracy=0.64, Precision=0.31, Recall=0.29, F1=0.30, normed F1=0.27

findings.finding_summary: Selective filtering improved the reliability of accepted AI-graded work. With a 50% partial-credit threshold, 47% of items were auto-accepted, mean absolute error on accepted items was 0.18 points, under-credit occurred on 11% of accepted items, under-credit greater than 0.25 points on 6%, over-credit on 25%, and bias was +0.08 points; total-score regression improved to slope=0.91, intercept=3.4, R²=0.96. Restricting acceptance to full-credit items yielded 27% coverage with MAE=0.12 and regression slope≈0.99, intercept=1.6, R²=0.98.
findings.measure: filtered AI grading performance under selective automation thresholds
findings.effect_size: At t=0.5: 47% accepted, MAE=0.18, Under=11%, Under >0.25=6%, Over=25%, Bias=0.08, slope=0.91, intercept=3.4, R²=0.96; at t=1.0: 27% accepted, MAE=0.12, slope≈0.99, intercept=1.6, R²=0.98

findings.finding_summary: The study concludes the AI system is promising for routine assessment tasks and can reduce grading burden, but is not reliable enough for unfiltered use in high-stakes handwritten chemistry exams. The authors emphasize the need for human oversight, especially for numerical, graphical, and ambiguous responses, and note concerns about student perceptions of fairness and trust.
findings.measure: practical suitability for deployment in high-stakes assessment

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical single-study evaluation with substantial quantitative analysis, but it is not an RCT or quasi-experimental study of student learning outcomes; it primarily examines grading reliability and workflow performance in one course context.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but mixed operational impact: strong efficiency and good alignment under filtering, but insufficient reliability for unfiltered high-stakes use and clear weaknesses on some task types. Effects are substantial in workflow terms but not reported as standardized educational outcome effects.
